title: Git and GitHub
moduleObjectives: Configure Git globally with `user.name`, `user.email`, and `init.defaultBranch` set to `main`
Initialize a repository and manage changes through the status / add / commit cycle with descriptive commit messages
Inspect changes and history confidently using `git status`, `git diff`, and `git log` with their most useful flags
Create, switch, merge, and delete branches, distinguishing fast-forward merges from true merge commits
Recover from common mistakes using `git restore`, `git restore --staged`, `git commit --amend`, and `git reset`
Generate an ed25519 SSH key, register it with a GitHub account, and push a local repository to a GitHub remote
Clone a repository from GitHub, pull updates, and resolve a merge conflict by hand
Open a pull request on GitHub, review and respond to inline comments, and merge it back to `main`

lessons.title: Prerequisites Check
lessons.objective: Verify that Git is installed and the Module 03 FastAPI project exists with no pre-existing `.git` directory.

lessons.title: Configure Git
lessons.objective: Configure Git globally with `user.name`, `user.email`, `init.defaultBranch=main`, and `pull.rebase=false`, then verify the settings stored in `~/.gitconfig`.

lessons.title: Init and First Commit
lessons.objective: Initialize a Git repository in the FastAPI project, extend `.gitignore`, stage everything with `git add .`, and make a first commit on `main`.

lessons.title: The status / add / commit Cycle
lessons.objective: Make a series of commits using the edit, `git status`, `git add`, `git commit` cycle, including selective staging and the `-am` shortcut's untracked-file limitation.

lessons.title: Diff and Log
lessons.objective: Inspect unstaged, staged, and between-commit changes with `git diff` and read history with `git log` filters such as `--oneline`, `--graph`, `--author`, and `--grep`.

lessons.title: Branches
lessons.objective: Create and switch branches with `git switch`, merge a feature branch into `main` via both a fast-forward and a true merge commit, and delete merged branches with `git branch -d`.

lessons.title: Undoing Things
lessons.objective: Undo common mistakes by discarding edits with `git restore`, unstaging with `git restore --staged`, amending the last commit with `git commit --amend`, and removing a commit with `git reset`.

lessons.title: GitHub Account and SSH Key
lessons.objective: Generate an ed25519 SSH key with `ssh-keygen`, register the public key in GitHub's settings, and verify passwordless authentication with `ssh -T`.

lessons.title: Pushing to GitHub
lessons.objective: Connect a local repository to a GitHub remote with `git remote add origin`, push it with `git push -u origin main`, and round-trip commits between the terminal and the web UI with `git push` and `git pull`.

lessons.title: Cloning, Pulling, and Conflicts
lessons.objective: Clone a repository from GitHub, sync changes between two working copies with `git pull`, and resolve a merge conflict by editing out the conflict markers, staging the file, and committing the merge.

lessons.title: Pull Requests
lessons.objective: Push a feature branch to GitHub, open a pull request, leave and respond to inline review comments, merge the PR with a merge commit, and sync the result to the local `main`.

lessons.title: Final Checkpoint
lessons.objective: Complete a full branch, commit, push, pull request, review, and merge cycle from memory and verify the new `/info` route works end to end.

quiz.question: Which command makes new repositories start on a `main` branch instead of `master`?
options: `git config --global init.defaultBranch main`
`git config --global branch.default main`
`git branch --set-default main`
`git init --default-branch main --global`
quiz.feedback: Lesson 01 sets `init.defaultBranch` globally so every future `git init` starts on `main`.

quiz.question: You edited `main.py`, ran `git commit -m "update"`, and Git reported nothing was committed. What step did you skip?
options: Running `git push` before committing
Staging the change with `git add main.py`
Re-running `git init` in the project
Setting `color.ui` to `auto` first
quiz.feedback: Changes must be staged with `git add` before `git commit` will include them — that is the core status / add / commit cycle.

quiz.question: You created a brand-new file `NOTES.md` and ran `git commit -am "Add notes file"`. What happens?
options: The file is committed along with any tracked changes
The file is staged but the commit is aborted
Nothing is committed — `-am` only stages files Git already tracks, so untracked files are skipped
Git prompts you to confirm adding the new file
quiz.feedback: Lesson 03 demonstrates that `-am` silently ignores untracked files, which still need a plain `git add` first.

quiz.question: After running `git add routers/items.py`, plain `git diff` shows no output. Which command shows the staged change?
options: `git diff --all`
`git log -p`
`git show HEAD`
`git diff --staged`
quiz.feedback: Plain `git diff` shows only unstaged working-tree changes; `git diff --staged` shows what is about to be committed.

quiz.question: When you merged `add-health-route` into `main`, Git reported "Fast-forward". What does that mean?
options: `main` had no commits of its own since the branch diverged, so Git just moved the `main` pointer forward with no merge commit
Git squashed the branch's commits into a single new commit
Git created a merge commit with two parent commits
Git replayed the branch's commits on top of `main` one at a time
quiz.feedback: A fast-forward happens when `main` hasn't diverged, so Git can simply advance the branch pointer without creating a merge commit.

quiz.question: You made an edit to `main.py` that you don't want to keep, and it is not staged. Which command discards it?
options: `git reset --soft HEAD`
`git restore main.py`
`git restore --staged main.py`
`git commit --amend --no-edit`
quiz.feedback: `git restore <file>` reverts a working-tree file to the version in the latest commit, which is the fix for an unwanted unstaged edit.

quiz.question: A `git pull` left `NOTES.md` with `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>>` markers. What is the correct way to finish the merge?
options: Run `git merge --continue` and let Git pick a side automatically
Run `git push --force` so your version wins
Edit the file to the final content, delete all the markers, then `git add NOTES.md` and `git commit`
Delete `NOTES.md` and run `git pull` again
quiz.feedback: Lesson 09 has you hand-edit the conflicted file, remove every marker, stage it with `git add`, and commit to conclude the merge.

quiz.question: When registering an SSH key with GitHub, what do you paste into Settings, SSH / GPG Keys?
options: The contents of `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` (the private key)
The contents of `~/.ssh/known_hosts`
The contents of `~/.gitconfig`
The contents of `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub` (the public key)
quiz.feedback: Only the public `.pub` key is uploaded to GitHub; the private key never leaves your machine.

quiz.question: Why do the lessons use `git push -u origin main` for the first push of a branch?
options: The `-u` sets the upstream tracking branch, so later pushes and pulls work with plain `git push` and `git pull`
The `-u` forces the push, overwriting any commits on the remote
The `-u` pushes every local branch at once
The `-u` uploads untracked files along with the commits
quiz.feedback: `-u` links the local branch to `origin/<branch>` so Git knows where to push and pull afterward without extra arguments.

quiz.question: Your `git push` is rejected with "the remote contains work that you do not have locally." What do the lessons say to do?
options: Run `git push --force` to overwrite the remote
Delete the GitHub repository and create it again
Run `git reset --hard` and redo your changes
Run `git pull` first, resolve any conflicts, then push again
quiz.feedback: The rejected push means the remote is ahead of you, so you pull (and resolve any conflicts) before pushing — never force-push over teammates' work.
